grammar.title: Letter names and sound checks
grammar.explanation: German spelling is relatively consistent, but letter names and umlauts differ from English. Spell in short groups, pause, and use a repair phrase when a sound is unclear.

grammar.commonMistake: Do not use English letter names when spelling German; German E, I, J, V, W, and Z sound especially different.

grammar.title: Core sound–spelling patterns
grammar.explanation: German spelling gives strong pronunciation clues: sch sounds like sh, z like ts, and w like v. The ch sound changes after front vowels such as i and back vowels such as a or u.
grammar.pattern: sch → sh · z → ts · w → v · ich-ch / Buch-ch
grammar.commonMistake: Do not pronounce German w as English w or German z as English z.

lines.translation: I would like to make an appointment.

lines.speaker: Rezeption
lines.text: Haben Sie am Mittwoch um zehn Uhr Zeit?
lines.translation: Do you have time on Wednesday at ten o'clock?

lines.speaker: Kunde

lines.speaker: Rezeption
lines.text: Ja, das passt. Mittwoch um elf Uhr.
lines.translation: Yes, that works. Wednesday at eleven o'clock.

lines.speaker: Kunde
lines.text: Vielen Dank. Auf Wiederhören!
lines.translation: Thank you very much. Goodbye!

questions.explanation: Der Termin means appointment.
Use am before a weekday.
They agree on Wednesday at eleven o'clock.
Der Mittwoch means Wednesday.
Pünktlich means on time or punctual.
Use um before an exact clock time.
Das passt confirms that the suggested time works.

questions.prompt: Why is ten o'clock not selected?
questions.explanation: The customer responds to ten o'clock with: Nein, leider nicht.

chapters.title: Wellbeing and plans

lessons.title: Everyday health basics
lessons.summary: Describe a common symptom and ask for simple help at a pharmacy.
lessons.heroTitle: Explain a simple health problem clearly.
lessons.completionTitle: You can ask for basic health help.
objectives: Name basic health places and symptoms
Describe common symptoms with haben
Understand simple pharmacy advice

sentences.note: Use sein with the adjective krank.
German normally uses haben to describe this symptom.
Tut weh is used with one body part; the prefix weh comes last.
Nächste identifies the nearest place.
A yes-or-no question begins with the conjugated verb.

grammar.title: Symptoms with haben
grammar.explanation: Use haben with many common symptoms such as Kopfschmerzen, Bauchschmerzen, or Fieber. Conjugate haben to match the person who feels unwell.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not use sein with a symptom noun; say ich habe Kopfschmerzen, not ich bin Kopfschmerzen.

lines.speaker: Apothekerin
lines.text: Guten Tag. Wie kann ich Ihnen helfen?
lines.translation: Good afternoon. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: Kunde
lines.text: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen.
lines.translation: I have a headache.

lines.speaker: Apothekerin
lines.text: Haben Sie auch Fieber?
lines.translation: Do you also have a fever?

lines.speaker: Kunde
lines.text: Nein, ich habe kein Fieber.
lines.translation: No, I do not have a fever.

lines.speaker: Apothekerin
lines.text: Trinken Sie viel Wasser und ruhen Sie sich aus.
lines.translation: Drink plenty of water and rest.

lines.speaker: Kunde
lines.text: Danke für Ihre Hilfe.
lines.translation: Thank you for your help.

questions.explanation: Die Apotheke means pharmacy.
German uses haben with Kopfschmerzen.

questions.prompt: What does the customer not have?
questions.explanation: The customer says: Ich habe kein Fieber.
Der Arzt means doctor.
Krank means ill or sick.
Use haben with the symptom Kopfschmerzen.
Tut weh means hurts.
The pharmacist recommends water and rest.

lessons.title: Weather and clothes
lessons.summary: Understand a simple forecast and choose suitable clothes for the day.
lessons.heroTitle: Dress for the day in German.
lessons.completionTitle: You can describe weather and choose clothing.
objectives: Describe basic weather conditions
Name useful clothes for warm and cold days
Use impersonal es in weather expressions

sentences.translation: What is the weather like today?
sentences.note: This is the standard basic question about the weather.
Impersonal es is the subject in many weather expressions.

sentences.translation: It will rain in the afternoon.
sentences.note: German commonly uses the present tense for a near-future forecast.
Mitnehmen separates into nimm ... mit in this informal instruction.

sentences.text: Ich trage einen Pullover und eine Jacke.
sentences.translation: I am wearing a sweater and a jacket.
sentences.note: Tragen is used for wearing clothes.

grammar.title: Impersonal es for weather
grammar.explanation: Weather expressions often use es as an impersonal subject. Use es ist with an adjective, or a weather verb such as regnen directly with es.
grammar.pattern: Es ist + adjective. / Es + weather verb.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not omit es in a basic weather sentence; say es ist kalt, not ist kalt.

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.text: Wie ist das Wetter heute?
lines.translation: What is the weather like today?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Am Morgen ist es warm und sonnig.
lines.translation: In the morning it is warm and sunny.

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.text: Brauche ich eine Jacke?
lines.translation: Do I need a jacket?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Ja. Am Nachmittag regnet es und es wird kalt.
lines.translation: Yes. In the afternoon it will rain and become cold.

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.text: Dann nehme ich eine Jacke mit.
lines.translation: Then I'll take a jacket with me.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Und vergiss den Regenschirm nicht!
lines.translation: And don't forget the umbrella!

questions.explanation: Die Jacke means jacket.
Weather descriptions use the impersonal subject es.
Tom says it will rain and become cold in the afternoon.
Das Wetter means weather.
Kalt, meaning cold, is the opposite of warm.
The weather verb regnen uses impersonal es.
Tragen means to wear or carry.
Tom tells Lena not to forget the umbrella.

lessons.title: Simple leisure plans
lessons.summary: Suggest a free-time activity and agree on where and when to meet.
lessons.heroTitle: Turn free time into a shared plan.
lessons.completionTitle: You can arrange a simple leisure activity.
objectives: Name familiar leisure activities
Make suggestions with wollen wir and können wir
Agree on a meeting place and time

sentences.translation: What are you doing at the weekend?
sentences.note: The present tense can describe a planned activity.

sentences.translation: Shall we go to the cinema?
sentences.note: Wollen wir ...? makes a direct shared suggestion.

sentences.text: Hast du Lust auf einen Spaziergang?
sentences.translation: Would you like to go for a walk?
sentences.note: Lust auf introduces an activity or thing someone might enjoy.

sentences.text: Wir können uns um sechs Uhr treffen.
sentences.translation: We can meet at six o'clock.
sentences.note: The infinitive treffen remains at the end after können.

sentences.text: Treffen wir uns vor dem Kino.
sentences.translation: Let's meet in front of the cinema.
sentences.note: This statement confirms the agreed meeting place.

grammar.title: Suggestions with wollen wir and können wir
grammar.explanation: Start with wollen wir to suggest a shared activity. Use wir können to offer a possible plan. With a modal verb, the activity verb stays as an infinitive at the end.
grammar.pattern: Wollen wir + ... + infinitive? / Wir können + ... + infinitive.

examples.translation: Shall we go for a walk?

grammar.commonMistake: Keep the activity verb at the end after the modal; say wir können ins Kino gehen.

lines.speaker: Mila
lines.text: Was machst du am Samstag?
lines.translation: What are you doing on Saturday?

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: Noch nichts. Wollen wir ins Kino gehen?
lines.translation: Nothing yet. Shall we go to the cinema?

lines.speaker: Mila
lines.text: Gern. Der Film beginnt um halb acht.
lines.translation: Gladly. The film begins at half past seven.

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: Dann können wir uns um sieben Uhr treffen.
lines.translation: Then we can meet at seven o'clock.

lines.speaker: Mila
lines.text: Gut. Treffen wir uns vor dem Kino.
lines.translation: Good. Let's meet in front of the cinema.

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: Bis Samstag!
lines.translation: See you Saturday!

questions.explanation: Das Wochenende means weekend.
The infinitive gehen comes at the end after wollen.

questions.prompt: Where will Mila and David meet?
questions.explanation: Mila suggests meeting in front of the cinema.
Die Freizeit means free time.
Spazieren gehen means to go for a walk.

questions.prompt: Shall we go to the cinema?
questions.explanation: Wollen wir begins the suggestion and gehen remains at the end.
The infinitive treffen follows können at the end.

questions.prompt: When will Mila and David meet?
questions.explanation: David suggests meeting at seven o'clock.

chapters.title: Calendar and identity
chapters.description: Talk about dates, languages and origin, and complete everyday personal-information forms.

lessons.title: Dates and birthdays
lessons.summary: Name weekdays and months, say a date, and ask when a birthday or event happens.
lessons.heroTitle: Put important days on the calendar.
lessons.completionTitle: You can understand and say simple dates.
objectives: Name common calendar units
Ask and answer when an event happens
Use ordinal dates after am

sentences.note: Welches matches the neuter noun Datum.

sentences.translation: Today is the third of May.
sentences.note: After ist, a spoken date commonly uses der plus the ordinal ending -te.
German uses haben: literally, when do you have birthday?

sentences.text: Ich habe am zwölften August Geburtstag.
sentences.translation: My birthday is on the twelfth of August.
sentences.note: After am, the ordinal date takes the ending -ten.
A day expression can appear without a preposition in this common time phrase.
Use im with seasons and months in general time expressions.

grammar.title: Ordinal dates with der and am
grammar.explanation: Use der plus an ordinal to state today's date. Use am plus an ordinal ending in -ten for most dates when saying when something happens.
grammar.pattern: Heute ist der dritte Mai. / am dritten Mai

examples.translation: Today is the first of June.

examples.source: Der Kurs beginnt am zehnten Juni.
examples.translation: The course starts on the tenth of June.

grammar.commonMistake: Do not use a plain counting number after am; say am dritten, not am drei.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.text: Wann hast du Geburtstag?
lines.translation: When is your birthday?

lines.speaker: Luis
lines.text: Am zwölften August.
lines.translation: On the twelfth of August.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.text: Feierst du am Wochenende?
lines.translation: Are you celebrating at the weekend?

lines.speaker: Luis
lines.text: Ja, die Feier ist am Samstag, dem vierzehnten August.
lines.translation: Yes, the celebration is on Saturday, the fourteenth of August.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.text: Um wie viel Uhr?
lines.translation: At what time?

lines.speaker: Luis
lines.text: Um sechs Uhr. Kommst du?
lines.translation: At six o'clock. Are you coming?

questions.explanation: Der Geburtstag means birthday.
After am, the ordinal takes -en: am dritten.
Luis gives Saturday, the fourteenth of August.
Der Monat means month.
Feiern means to celebrate.
Use am plus the ordinal ending -ten.
Wann asks when, and German uses Geburtstag haben.

questions.prompt: What time does the celebration begin?
questions.explanation: Luis says: Um sechs Uhr.

lessons.title: Countries and languages
lessons.summary: Say where you come from, where you live, and which languages you speak.
lessons.heroTitle: Share where you come from and how you communicate.
lessons.completionTitle: You can talk about origin and languages.
objectives: Name selected countries and languages
Use aus for origin and in for residence
Conjugate sprechen in common forms

sentences.note: Woher asks about origin or direction from a place.
Use aus before most country names without an article.
Use in for the country where you live.
Sprichst is the vowel-changing du form of sprechen.
Language names are capitalized and normally used without an article.

sentences.translation: I am learning a little German.
sentences.note: Ein bisschen is a useful way to describe limited ability.

grammar.title: Origin with aus and residence with in
grammar.explanation: Use kommen aus to say where someone comes from and wohnen in to say where someone lives. Most country names appear without an article in these basic phrases.
grammar.pattern: kommen aus + country / wohnen in + country or city
grammar.commonMistake: Do not use von for basic national origin; the standard phrase is ich komme aus.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Hallo, ich heiße Ana. Woher kommst du?
lines.translation: Hello, my name is Ana. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Yusuf
lines.text: Ich komme aus Ägypten, aber ich wohne jetzt in Köln.
lines.translation: I come from Egypt, but I live in Cologne now.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Welche Sprachen sprichst du?
lines.translation: Which languages do you speak?

lines.speaker: Yusuf
lines.text: Arabisch, Englisch und ein bisschen Deutsch. Und du?
lines.translation: Arabic, English, and a little German. And you?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Ich komme aus Spanien und spreche Spanisch und Deutsch.
lines.translation: I come from Spain and speak Spanish and German.

lines.speaker: Yusuf
lines.text: Dann können wir zusammen Deutsch üben.
lines.translation: Then we can practise German together.

questions.explanation: Arabisch means Arabic.
Kommen aus expresses origin.
Yusuf says that he now lives in Köln.
Deutschland means Germany.
Sprechen means to speak.
Wohnen in describes residence.
Sprechen changes its vowel in the du form: du sprichst.
Ana says: Spanisch und Deutsch.

lessons.title: Forms and contact details
lessons.summary: Understand common form fields and give complete contact information accurately.
lessons.heroTitle: Turn your details into a complete form.
lessons.completionTitle: You can complete a basic personal-information form.
objectives: Recognize common personal-information fields
Give an email address and postcode
Use nicht and kein for missing information

sentences.text: Bitte füllen Sie dieses Formular aus.
sentences.note: In a formal instruction, ausfüllen separates into füllen ... aus.
Say Punkt for a dot and at for the @ sign in an email address.

sentences.text: Meine Postleitzahl ist fünf null sechs sieben acht.
sentences.note: Long numbers such as postcodes are often spoken digit by digit.

sentences.translation: I do not have a German telephone number.
sentences.note: Keine negates the feminine noun Telefonnummer.
Nicht negates the adjective wichtig.
The formal imperative places Sie after the verb.

grammar.title: Negation with kein and nicht
grammar.explanation: Use kein before an indefinite noun or a noun without an article. Use nicht to negate an adjective, verb, definite noun, or the wider statement.
grammar.pattern: kein/e + noun / nicht + adjective or statement

examples.translation: I do not have a telephone number.

grammar.commonMistake: Do not use nicht directly where English uses no before a noun; use the matching form of kein.

lines.speaker: Mitarbeiterin
lines.text: Bitte füllen Sie dieses Formular aus.
lines.translation: Please fill in this form.

lines.speaker: Samir
lines.text: Was schreibe ich in dieses Feld?
lines.translation: What do I write in this field?

lines.speaker: Mitarbeiterin
lines.text: Dort schreiben Sie Ihre Staatsangehörigkeit.
lines.translation: You write your nationality there.

lines.speaker: Samir
lines.text: Ich habe keine deutsche Telefonnummer.
lines.translation: I do not have a German telephone number.

lines.speaker: Mitarbeiterin
lines.text: Das ist kein Problem. Ihre E-Mail-Adresse reicht.
lines.translation: That is not a problem. Your email address is sufficient.

lines.speaker: Samir
lines.text: Gut. Wo muss ich unterschreiben?
lines.translation: Good. Where do I have to sign?

questions.explanation: Die Postleitzahl means postcode.
Telefonnummer is feminine, so the negative article is keine.

questions.prompt: What can Samir provide instead of a German phone number?
questions.explanation: The employee says his email address is sufficient.
Die Unterschrift means signature.
Ausfüllen means to fill in a form.
Nicht negates the adjective wichtig.
Ausfüllen separates into füllen ... aus.

questions.prompt: Which detail does Samir not have?
questions.explanation: Samir says he has no German telephone number.

chapters.title: Work and study
chapters.description: Use classroom language, talk about learning habits, and handle simple workplace conversations.

lessons.title: In the classroom
lessons.summary: Identify classroom items, follow basic instructions, and ask when something is unclear.
lessons.heroTitle: Understand what happens in class.
lessons.completionTitle: You can follow and ask about classroom tasks.
objectives: Name essential classroom items
Follow common classroom instructions
Use definite articles and plural forms

sentences.text: Öffnen Sie bitte das Buch auf Seite zehn.
sentences.translation: Please open the book on page ten.
sentences.note: The formal instruction begins with the verb and places Sie next.

sentences.text: Lesen Sie den Text und beantworten Sie die Fragen.
sentences.translation: Read the text and answer the questions.
sentences.note: Und connects two instructions with the same formal register.

sentences.translation: I do not understand the exercise.
sentences.note: Nicht comes after the object when it negates the whole action here.
A useful question for independent learning.
Können Sie ...? makes a polite classroom request.
This is an informal plural instruction addressed to a group.

grammar.title: Definite articles and plural nouns
grammar.explanation: German singular nouns use der, die, or das according to gender. Every plural noun uses die in the nominative and accusative, although the noun's plural ending varies.
grammar.pattern: der Stift · die Seite · das Heft · die Stifte/Seiten/Hefte
grammar.commonMistake: Learn every noun with its article and plural; German plurals do not follow one universal ending.

lines.speaker: Lehrerin
lines.text: Öffnen Sie bitte das Buch auf Seite zwölf.
lines.translation: Please open the book on page twelve.

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Entschuldigung, ich verstehe die Aufgabe nicht.
lines.translation: Excuse me, I do not understand the exercise.

lines.speaker: Lehrerin
lines.text: Kein Problem. Lesen Sie zuerst den Text.
lines.translation: No problem. First read the text.

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Und dann beantworte ich die Fragen?
lines.translation: And then do I answer the questions?

lines.speaker: Lehrerin
lines.text: Ja, genau. Arbeiten Sie danach zu zweit.
lines.translation: Yes, exactly. After that, work in pairs.

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Danke, jetzt verstehe ich es.
lines.translation: Thank you, now I understand it.

questions.explanation: Die Aufgabe means exercise or task.
All plural nouns use die in the nominative and accusative.
The teacher says: Lesen Sie zuerst den Text.
Das Heft means notebook.
Verstehen means to understand.
Stift is masculine, Seite feminine, and Heft neuter.
Können Sie plus an infinitive forms a polite request.

questions.prompt: When does Omar understand the task?
choices: After the teacher explains the steps
questions.correctAnswer: After the teacher explains the steps
questions.explanation: At the end he says: Jetzt verstehe ich es.

lessons.title: Learning and study habits
lessons.summary: Describe what and how you study using complete present-tense verb patterns.
lessons.heroTitle: Build a study routine that speaks German.
lessons.completionTitle: You can describe simple learning habits.
objectives: Name common study activities
Conjugate regular verbs across subject pronouns
Say what you like doing with gern

sentences.text: Ich lerne jeden Tag zwanzig Minuten Deutsch.
sentences.translation: I study German for twenty minutes every day.
sentences.note: A duration can appear without a preposition.

sentences.text: Du übst neue Wörter und Sätze.
sentences.translation: You practise new words and sentences.
sentences.note: Regular verbs take -st with du.
Lesen changes e to ie in the er/sie/es form: liest.

sentences.text: Wir hören morgens einen deutschen Podcast.
sentences.translation: We listen to a German podcast in the morning.
sentences.note: The wir form matches the infinitive: hören.

sentences.translation: Are you all doing the homework today?
sentences.note: The ihr form of a regular verb ends in -t.

sentences.text: Im Kurs sprechen wir viel Deutsch.
sentences.translation: In the course we speak a lot of German.
sentences.note: The opening place phrase is followed by the verb, then the subject.

grammar.title: Regular verbs in the present tense
grammar.explanation: Remove -en from a regular infinitive and add endings that match the subject: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. The formal Sie form matches the infinitive and is capitalized.
grammar.pattern: ich lerne · du lernst · er/sie lernt · wir lernen · ihr lernt · sie/Sie lernen
grammar.commonMistake: Do not use the infinitive with every subject; the verb ending must match the subject.

lines.speaker: Mina
lines.text: Wie lernst du Deutsch?
lines.translation: How do you study German?

lines.speaker: Jon
lines.text: Ich übe jeden Tag neue Wörter.
lines.translation: I practise new words every day.

lines.speaker: Mina
lines.text: Liest du auch deutsche Texte?
lines.translation: Do you also read German texts?

lines.speaker: Jon
lines.text: Ja, aber nur kurze Texte. Abends höre ich gern Podcasts.
lines.translation: Yes, but only short texts. In the evening I like listening to podcasts.

lines.speaker: Mina
lines.text: Wir können morgen zusammen sprechen üben.
lines.translation: We can practise speaking together tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Jon
lines.text: Gute Idee!
lines.translation: Good idea!

questions.explanation: Üben means to practise.
The du ending of a regular verb is -st.

questions.prompt: What does Jon like doing in the evening?
questions.explanation: Jon says: Abends höre ich gern Podcasts.
Die Hausaufgabe means homework.
Täglich means daily.
The wir form matches the infinitive: lernen.
The er/sie/es form of lesen is liest.

questions.prompt: What will Mina and Jon practise together?
questions.explanation: Mina suggests practising speaking together.

lessons.title: A simple workday
lessons.summary: Talk about a job, colleagues, a work schedule, and simple reasons or contrasts.
lessons.heroTitle: Describe the people and rhythm of a workday.
lessons.completionTitle: You can talk about a simple workday.
objectives: Name basic workplace people and places
Describe a work schedule
Connect ideas with und, aber, and denn

sentences.note: This is a standard formal question about someone's job.

sentences.text: Ich arbeite in einem kleinen Büro.
sentences.translation: I work in a small office.
sentences.note: In einem describes a location inside a neuter place.

sentences.text: Meine Arbeitszeit beginnt um acht Uhr.
sentences.translation: My working hours begin at eight o'clock.
sentences.note: The singular subject Arbeitszeit takes beginnt.

sentences.text: Um zehn Uhr haben wir eine Besprechung.
sentences.translation: At ten o'clock we have a meeting.
sentences.note: The time phrase comes first, so the verb precedes the subject.

sentences.text: Meine Kollegen sind freundlich und helfen gern.
sentences.translation: My colleagues are friendly and like to help.
sentences.note: Gern describes an activity someone likes doing.

sentences.text: Ich fahre mit dem Bus, denn das Büro ist weit weg.
sentences.translation: I travel by bus because the office is far away.
sentences.note: Denn gives a reason without changing main-clause word order.

grammar.title: Connecting ideas with und, aber, and denn
grammar.explanation: Use und to add information, aber to show a contrast, and denn to give a reason. Each connector joins main clauses without moving the conjugated verb to the end.

examples.source: Ich arbeite und meine Kollegin studiert.
examples.translation: I work and my colleague studies.

examples.source: Ich fahre mit dem Bus, denn der Weg ist weit.
examples.translation: I go by bus because the journey is long.

grammar.commonMistake: Keep normal main-clause order after denn; the verb does not move to the end as it does after weil.

lines.speaker: Lea
lines.text: Guten Morgen. Ich bin Lea, die neue Kollegin.
lines.translation: Good morning. I am Lea, the new colleague.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Willkommen! Ich heiße Ben und arbeite auch hier im Büro.
lines.translation: Welcome! My name is Ben and I also work here in the office.

lines.speaker: Lea
lines.text: Wann beginnt die Besprechung?
lines.translation: When does the meeting begin?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Um zehn Uhr, aber wir trinken zuerst einen Kaffee.
lines.translation: At ten o'clock, but first we have a coffee.

lines.speaker: Lea
lines.text: Gut. Kannst du mir später helfen?
lines.translation: Good. Can you help me later?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Natürlich. Frag mich einfach.
lines.translation: Of course. Just ask me.

questions.explanation: Die Besprechung means meeting.

questions.prompt: Ich fahre mit dem Bus, ___ das Büro ist weit weg.
questions.explanation: Denn introduces the reason.
Ben says they drink coffee first.
Das Büro means office.
Helfen means to help.

questions.prompt: Das Büro ist klein, ___ sehr schön.
questions.explanation: Aber introduces a contrast.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct order after denn.
questions.prompt: I take the bus because the office is far away.
choices: Ich fahre mit dem Bus, denn das Büro ist weit weg.
Ich fahre mit dem Bus, denn weit weg das Büro ist.
Ich fahre mit dem Bus, denn das Büro weit weg.

Lea introduces herself as the new colleague.

chapters.title: Home and neighborhood
chapters.description: Describe rooms and furniture, locate places nearby, and use essential public services.

lessons.title: Rooms and furniture
lessons.summary: Describe a home, name essential furniture, and say what a room contains.
lessons.heroTitle: Make every room part of your German.
lessons.completionTitle: You can describe the main parts of a home.
objectives: Name common rooms and furniture
Describe what a room contains with es gibt
Use simple size and condition adjectives

sentences.note: Hat agrees with the singular subject Wohnung.

sentences.text: Es gibt ein Wohnzimmer und zwei Schlafzimmer.
sentences.translation: There is a living room and there are two bedrooms.
sentences.note: Es gibt introduces both singular and plural things.

sentences.text: Im Schlafzimmer gibt es ein Bett und einen Schrank.
sentences.translation: In the bedroom there is a bed and a wardrobe.
sentences.note: Es gibt always takes an accusative object: ein Bett, einen Schrank.

sentences.text: Die Küche ist klein, aber praktisch.
sentences.translation: The kitchen is small but practical.
sentences.note: Predicative adjectives after ist have no ending.

sentences.text: Das Wohnzimmer ist hell und gemütlich.
sentences.translation: The living room is bright and cosy.
sentences.note: Und joins two equal descriptions.

sentences.translation: Unfortunately, we do not have a balcony.
sentences.note: Keinen is the masculine accusative form of kein.

grammar.title: Describing what exists with es gibt
grammar.explanation: Use es gibt to say that something exists or is available. The noun after es gibt is accusative, so masculine ein becomes einen and kein becomes keinen.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not change gibt for plural objects; es gibt stays the same with one or many things.

lines.speaker: Maklerin
lines.text: Die Wohnung hat drei Zimmer und einen Balkon.
lines.translation: The apartment has three rooms and a balcony.

lines.speaker: Nora
lines.text: Ist das Wohnzimmer hell?

lessons.title: Where things are
lessons.summary: Locate objects and places using common two-way prepositions with the dative case.
lessons.heroTitle: Say exactly where something is.
lessons.completionTitle: You can describe basic locations accurately.
objectives: Use common location prepositions
Choose dative articles after wo
Understand contractions such as im and am

sentences.text: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
sentences.translation: The book is lying on the table.
sentences.note: A fixed location after auf uses the dative: dem Tisch.

sentences.text: Die Lampe steht neben dem Bett.
sentences.translation: The lamp stands next to the bed.
sentences.note: Neben takes the dative when answering wo.

sentences.text: Der Schrank steht zwischen der Tür und dem Fenster.
sentences.translation: The wardrobe is between the door and the window.
sentences.note: Feminine die becomes der and neuter das becomes dem in the dative.

sentences.text: Die Schuhe sind unter dem Stuhl.
sentences.translation: The shoes are under the chair.
sentences.note: Sein is also natural for a simple location.

sentences.text: Die Bushaltestelle ist vor dem Supermarkt.
sentences.translation: The bus stop is in front of the supermarket.
sentences.note: Vor dem locates one place relative to another.
Wo asks for a fixed location and leads to dative location phrases.

grammar.title: Location with two-way prepositions
grammar.explanation: When auf, neben, zwischen, unter, vor, or hinter answers wo, use the dative case. Der and das become dem; die becomes der; plural die becomes den.

examples.source: Der Schlüssel liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.translation: The key is on the table.

examples.source: Die Bank ist neben der Post.
examples.translation: The bank is next to the post office.

grammar.commonMistake: Use dative for a fixed location; accusative is used later for movement toward a destination.

sentences.translation: Where is the nearest post office?

sentences.text: Die Bank ist neben dem Rathaus.

grammar.title: Opening hours with von and bis
grammar.explanation: Use von for the starting time and bis for the ending time. With exact clock times, von ... bis ... normally appears without repeating um.

lessons.title: Meals and preferences
lessons.summary: Describe daily meals and say what you like, dislike, or prefer to eat and drink.
lessons.heroTitle: Talk naturally about what you enjoy eating.
lessons.completionTitle: You can describe meals and food preferences.
objectives: Name daily meals and basic needs
Use mögen with nouns and gern with activities
Compare preferences with lieber

sentences.text: Zum Frühstück esse ich Brot und Obst.
sentences.translation: For breakfast I eat bread and fruit.
sentences.note: Zum Frühstück introduces the meal context.

sentences.text: Ich habe Hunger, aber keinen Durst.
sentences.translation: I am hungry, but I am not thirsty.
sentences.note: German literally says I have hunger and thirst.
Mag is the ich form of mögen and takes a noun object.

sentences.translation: I like cooking in the evening.
sentences.note: Gern modifies the activity expressed by the verb.

sentences.text: Trinkst du lieber Tee oder Kaffee?
sentences.translation: Do you prefer drinking tea or coffee?
sentences.note: Lieber compares preferred activities or choices.

sentences.text: Am Wochenende essen wir zusammen zu Abend.
sentences.translation: At the weekend we eat dinner together.
sentences.note: Zu Abend essen is a common expression for having dinner.

grammar.title: Likes and preferences with mögen, gern, and lieber
grammar.explanation: Use mögen with a noun to say you like something. Use a verb plus gern for an activity you like doing. Replace gern with lieber when you prefer one activity or choice.
grammar.pattern: ich mag + noun / ich + verb + gern / ich + verb + lieber

examples.source: Ich trinke gern Tee, aber lieber Wasser.
examples.translation: I like drinking tea, but I prefer water.

grammar.commonMistake: Do not put gern directly before a noun; say ich mag Pizza or ich esse gern Pizza.

Use the activity verb plus gern.

Order naturally with ich hätte gern

sentences.text: Kann ich bitte die Speisekarte haben?

sentences.translation: I would like the vegetable soup.

grammar.explanation: Treat ich hätte gern as a complete polite phrase meaning I would like. It can be followed directly by a noun phrase and sounds natural in restaurants and shops.

questions.explanation: Die Rechnung means bill.

grammar.title: Pointing out items with dieser

lessons.title: At the train station
lessons.summary: Buy the right ticket and understand basic departure information at a station.
lessons.heroTitle: Start a train journey with confidence.
lessons.completionTitle: You can buy a ticket and find your train.
objectives: Name essential station information
Ask for a single or return ticket
Use destination phrases with nach and zu

sentences.note: Use nach with cities and most countries without an article.

sentences.translation: One way or return as well?
sentences.note: This is a common compact question at a ticket counter.

sentences.text: Wann fährt der nächste Zug ab?
sentences.translation: When does the next train depart?
sentences.note: Abfahren separates into fährt ... ab in a main-clause question.

sentences.text: Der Zug fährt um neun Uhr von Bahnsteig vier.
sentences.translation: The train leaves at nine from platform four.
sentences.note: Von identifies the departure point.

sentences.translation: Do I have to change trains in Cologne?
sentences.note: The separable infinitive remains together after muss.

sentences.text: Nein, der Zug fährt direkt nach Bonn.
sentences.translation: No, the train goes directly to Bonn.
sentences.note: Direkt means no change is needed.

grammar.title: Destinations with nach and zu
grammar.explanation: Use nach for cities, compass directions, and most countries without an article. Use zu for people and many local destinations, usually contracted to zum or zur.
grammar.pattern: nach Berlin/Deutschland · zum Bahnhof/Arzt · zur Post

examples.translation: I am going to the train station.

grammar.commonMistake: Do not use nach before a person or ordinary local service; use zu, zum, or zur.

lessons.heroTitle: Find your way one clear step at a time.
lessons.completionTitle: You can ask for and follow simple directions.
objectives: Understand direction and distance words
Give formal directions with the imperative
Distinguish fixed location from movement destination

sentences.text: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Museum?
sentences.translation: Excuse me, how do I get to the museum?
sentences.note: Wie komme ich zu ...? is a standard route question.
The formal imperative begins with the verb and then Sie.

sentences.text: Biegen Sie an der Ampel links ab.
sentences.translation: Turn left at the traffic light.
sentences.note: The separable prefix ab moves to the end of the instruction.

sentences.text: Überqueren Sie die Straße an der Kreuzung.
sentences.translation: Cross the street at the intersection.

sentences.text: Das Museum ist auf der rechten Seite.
sentences.translation: The museum is on the right-hand side.
sentences.note: Auf der uses dative for the fixed location.

grammar.title: Formal directions with the imperative
grammar.explanation: For a formal instruction, place the infinitive-shaped verb first and Sie immediately after it. A separable prefix still moves to the end.
